findings.title: resolve() deletes live links on every hit
findings.description: The check `Instant.now().isBefore(link.expiresAt)` is true exactly when the link is still valid. The branch then removes the link from the map and returns null, so every valid link resolves to null on the first hit. Expired links fall through to the `link.hits++; return link.target` path, so expired links resolve successfully and live ones cannot.

findings.title: prune() mutates the map while iterating its keySet
findings.description: `for (String code : links.keySet()) { ... links.remove(code); ... }` modifies the very map whose keySet view is being iterated. On any non-empty store this throws ConcurrentModificationException and the janitor tick (and any direct caller) crashes.

findings.title: Janitor mutates Store.all() while iterating its keySet
findings.description: `for (String code : store.all().keySet()) { ... store.all().remove(code); }` mutates the underlying map during iteration, throwing ConcurrentModificationException on the first expired entry. The janitor thread dies and never sweeps again.

findings.title: redirect() NPEs when ?code= is missing
findings.description: `query(exchange).get("code")` returns null for a request without a `code` query parameter, and the very next line calls `code.toLowerCase()`. The handler NPEs instead of returning a 400.

findings.title: stats() divides by store.size() without guarding zero
findings.description: `long perLink = hits / store.size();` runs on every /stats hit. When the store is empty (cold start or right after `prune` empties it) this is `hits / 0`, which throws ArithmeticException and kills the request.

findings.title: warmCache leaks its ExecutorService and returns before work finishes
findings.description: `warmCache` builds an 8-thread pool, submits tasks, and falls off the end without `shutdown()` and without awaiting termination. Threads keep running (and prevent JVM exit) and the docstring claim "Returns after every probe has finished" is false.

findings.title: requireAdmin rejects admins
findings.description: `if (!session.role.equals("admin") || !session.role.equals("owner")) return false;` — a single string can never equal both "admin" and "owner", so the second operand is always true and the whole expression is `!"admin" || true` = true for any role. Every admin call is rejected. The intent is clearly to require the role to be `admin` (or both checks should be `&&`).

findings.title: verify() compares tokens with `==`
findings.description: `if (session.token == token)` is reference equality on String. Tokens issued via `Long.toHexString(random.nextLong())` are not interned, so the presented token will never be `==` to a stored token and every verify() returns null — the entire auth surface rejects every caller.

findings.title: bearerToken() NPEs on a missing or single-word header
findings.description: `header.split(" ")` and then unconditionally `return parts[1]` throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for any header that is null, empty, or just a single token. Every endpoint that calls `authenticate` therefore crashes the request thread on malformed input.

findings.title: byOwner() uses contains() and leaks other users' links
findings.description: `if (link.owner.contains(owner))` matches when the supplied `owner` string appears anywhere inside `link.owner`. A user who supplies a substring (e.g. their own prefix or an empty string) gets every owner's links back, not just their own. This is both a logic error and a data-disclosure bug in normal use.

findings.title: exportCsv() allows path traversal through `name`
findings.description: `new File(dir, name + ".csv")` does not sanitize `name`. A caller passing `../../etc/passwd` (or `..\..\foo`) writes outside `dir`. The docstring promises `name` is "confined to dir" but nothing enforces it. `Main.report` exposes this directly to authenticated users.

findings.title: page() off-by-one can throw IndexOutOfBoundsException
findings.description: When the requested window overflows the end, the code sets `end = all.size() + 1` instead of `end = all.size()`. `subList(offset, all.size() + 1)` then throws IndexOutOfBoundsException whenever any link exists and the page extends past the end.

findings.title: successRate() always reports 0 or 100
findings.description: `return used / links.size() * 100;` evaluates `used / links.size()` with integer division first, then multiplies by 100. Any ratio below 1.0 collapses to 0; only a 100% hit rate reports 100. The dashboard metric is meaningless for every value between.

findings.title: create() NPEs for new owners via auto-unboxing
findings.description: `quota.put(owner, quota.get(owner) + 1)` auto-unboxes the `Integer` returned by `get`. For a first-time owner the map returns `null`, unboxing throws NullPointerException, and the create request crashes after the link was already inserted.

findings.title: quotas() returns the live internal map, contradicting the doc
findings.description: `return quota;` hands callers the same `HashMap` the store mutates. The Javadoc claims it is a snapshot and "mutating it must not affect the store" — that is false. Any caller can clear or rewrite quota counts.

findings.title: Metrics.addCreated() is not synchronized
findings.description: `addResolved()` and `snapshot()` are synchronized, but `addCreated()` is not. `Main.links` is served by the HttpServer's request threads, so concurrent POSTs race on the `created++` and can lose increments or observe torn values from `snapshot()`.

findings.title: findByCode() compares codes with `==`
findings.description: `if (link.code == code)` uses reference equality on String. Codes are minted by `Long.toHexString(random.nextLong()).substring(0, 8)` and not interned, so this method will fail to find any link whose code was stored as a non-interned String.

findings.title: set() exceeds the cache limit on every full insert
findings.description: When the cache is at `limit`, `set` removes exactly one entry (the iterator's first) and then unconditionally calls `entries.put`. Each `set` past capacity replaces one entry and adds another, so the cache can grow without bound under steady insert pressure. Eviction is also not LRU as documented.

findings.title: utilization() reports 0 until the cache is completely full
findings.description: `return entries.size() / limit * 100;` is integer division. With limit=1024 and 500 entries it returns 0; only at exactly 1024 entries does it report 100. The dashboard meter is effectively binary.

findings.title: Bad LINKD_TIMEOUT_MS zeroes the timeout, then validate() fails
findings.description: A `NumberFormatException` from `Integer.parseInt(timeout)` sets `cfg.timeoutMillis = 0` and logs a warning. `validate()` then refuses `timeoutMillis <= 0`, but `validate()` always returns true (see next finding) so the service silently starts with timeout=0.

findings.title: LINKD_CACHE_TTL_MS parse error is uncaught
findings.description: `Long.parseLong(ttl)` is not wrapped in try/catch. A non-numeric value (e.g. `5m`) throws NumberFormatException out of `Config.load()` and aborts startup. The sibling `LINKD_PORT` parse path at least catches and falls back.

findings.title: LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT bounds check is a no-op
findings.description: `if (parsed > 0) { parsed = parsed; }` is dead code: the assignment is a self-assignment, so non-positive values are still stored on `cfg.fetchLimit`. The intent was clearly to either clamp or reject non-positive input.

findings.title: validate() always reports success
findings.description: `return true;` runs regardless of `problems`, so the log line is the only signal a bad config produced. `Main.main` calls `validate()` and proceeds to bind to the port unconditionally.

findings.title: rename() validates the wrong variable twice
findings.description: Lines 51 and 52 both call `validateCode(from)`. The second call should be `validateCode(to)`, leaving `to` unchecked (any string, including a duplicate, can be supplied without complaint until the explicit containsKey check fires).

findings.title: writeSnapshot() rename is unreliable across filesystems
findings.description: `tmp` lives under `/tmp`; `renameTo` is not guaranteed to work when source and destination are on different filesystems (and silently fails). On any non-tmpfs deploy the snapshot never lands in `dir`. There is also no error handling.

findings.title: Unsynchronized HashMap accessed by multiple HTTP handler threads and the janitor
findings.description: All Store methods (create, resolve, delete, extend, prune, rename, page, top, byOwner, totalHits, quotas, all) read and write the `links` and `quota` HashMaps with no synchronization. Multiple HTTP handler threads mutate these maps concurrently, and the janitor thread iterates store.all() while handlers mutate, causing ConcurrentModificationException, HashMap corruption (NPE/infinite loop on resize), and lost updates.

findings.title: Sessions HashMap accessed from every HTTP thread without synchronization
findings.description: `sessions` is read and written by `issue`, `verify`, and `revoke` with no synchronization. Every HTTP request calls `verify` while other threads call `issue`/`revoke`, producing data races on the HashMap: NPE on missing bucket, infinite loop during rehash, and lost session entries.

findings.title: `peek` reads `entries` without synchronization while mutators are synchronized
findings.description: `peek` (and `utilization`, `stats`) read `entries.containsKey`/`entries.size`/counters without holding the lock, while `get`/`set`/`delete`/`sweep` mutate `entries` under `synchronized`. A concurrent `set` can resize the HashMap while `peek` is reading, producing NPE on a null bucket or an infinite loop on rehash.

findings.title: Janitor thread iterates a live, unsynchronized HashMap
findings.description: `startJanitor` runs a loop that calls `store.all()` and iterates the result while HTTP handlers concurrently call `create`/`delete`/`extend`/`prune` on the same underlying HashMap. Iteration without synchronization triggers ConcurrentModificationException and HashMap corruption, with no recovery path.

findings.title: Double-checked locking in `getInstance` is not safe
findings.description: `getInstance` reads and assigns `instance` without `volatile` and outside any synchronization, so concurrent callers can each observe a partially-constructed Cache and publish two distinct singletons. Because the class relies on `synchronized` instance state, two instances mean inconsistent state.

findings.title: Metrics counters are not synchronized between writers and snapshot
findings.description: `Metrics.addCreated` increments `created` without synchronization while `Metrics.snapshot` reads it concurrently. The same pattern likely applies to other counters. Writers and readers race, producing torn or stale values in snapshots and the metrics endpoint.

findings.title: `warmCache` leaks the executor and ignores its Javadoc contract
findings.description: `warmCache` submits probes to an ExecutorService and returns without calling `shutdown()` or `awaitTermination()`. The pool's worker threads stay alive indefinitely, and probes may still be in flight when `warmCache` returns, contradicting the Javadoc that says it returns after every probe has finished.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback secret allows token forgery
findings.description: When LINKD_SECRET is unset or empty, the authenticator silently falls back to the literal string 'dev-secret-do-not-use'. Anyone with source access (e.g. a leaked binary, an open repo, the default Docker image) knows this value and can forge sessions through issue() or any code path that trusts session.role. The env var is also the secret used by secretEquals(), so a missing var means authentication-equivalent operations are validated against a value every reader of the source possesses.

findings.title: Admin gate is a client-controlled header
findings.description: The /admin/quotas handler trusts the X-Admin request header ('if (!"true".equals(admin)) ... 403'). Any authenticated session — including a freshly-issued non-admin token — can flip this header to 'true' and read the per-owner quota map. The Authenticator's role/owner fields are never consulted; requireAdmin() is defined but never called, so the only check is a value the attacker supplies.

findings.title: Path traversal in exportCsv/readReport/archiveAll
findings.description: new File(dir, name + ".csv") accepts name strings like '../../../etc/cron.d/evil' because java.io.File does not normalize or sandbox the path segment. exportCsv is reachable from /report with a session token, so any authenticated user can write a CSV anywhere the JVM can write — including overwriting config files in cfg.exportDir's parent, planting cron jobs, or replacing the snapshot.json with attacker bytes. readReport then lets the same caller read those files back via the response body. archiveAll's entry.getKey() in the file name lets a poisoned owner label do the same on import.

findings.title: DELETE /links bypasses owner check
findings.description: The comment claims 'A link may only be deleted by the user who created it', but the handler authenticates the caller and then calls store.delete(code) without comparing session.owner to link.owner. Any authenticated user can DELETE any link, deleting another tenant's data and freeing their quota slot. This is a horizontal-privilege-escalation / DoS primitive against other owners.

findings.title: Open redirect on /out?next=
findings.description: /out reads the user-controlled 'next' parameter and returns it verbatim in the Location header with a 301. An attacker can craft short links of the form /out?next=https://evil.example.com/phish and distribute them as if they came from the service. Combined with the link-shortener's domain reputation this is a phishing primitive.

findings.title: Session tokens are predictable (java.util.Random)
findings.description: issue() builds tokens from Long.toHexString(random.nextLong()). java.util.Random is a 48-bit LCG with publicly-known state transitions; observing a handful of issued tokens is enough to recover the seed and predict subsequent tokens, letting an attacker forge sessions for arbitrary owners without knowing the secret.

findings.title: verify() ignores session.expiresAt
findings.description: verify() scans sessions for a matching token but never compares Instant.now() to session.expiresAt. A stolen token continues to authenticate indefinitely; revoke() is the only way to invalidate it. Combined with the predictable-RNG finding above, an attacker who learns or guesses a token can use it forever.

findings.title: Password hashing is unsalted SHA-256
findings.description: hashPassword() runs SHA-256 once over the password bytes with no salt and no work factor. Identical passwords produce identical hashes, so a stolen user table falls to rainbow tables and a single GPU pass. This is the right shape for an integrity check, not for stored credentials.

findings.title: CORS allows wildcard origin with credentials
findings.description: respond() sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true on every response. The combination is rejected by browsers per spec, but if any frontend ever downgrades to allow_credentials=true with a reflecting proxy or a mis-set '*', user credentials would be exposed cross-origin. It also advertises a permissive default for any future code that leans on it.

findings.title: Short codes are predictable (java.util.Random)
findings.description: newCode() takes 8 hex chars from random.nextLong() — the same non-cryptographic Random used for tokens. The 32-bit space combined with a recoverable seed makes pre-image prediction feasible: an attacker who can observe a few issued codes can predict subsequent codes and pre-register or hijack them.

findings.title: secretEquals is timing-vulnerable
findings.description: secretEquals() uses String.equals, which short-circuits on the first mismatched byte. Over a network an attacker can stage a timing oracle to recover the expected secret one byte at a time. The doc comment claims 'without leaking how much of it matched' — the implementation does the opposite.

findings.title: Issued session tokens are written to stdout
findings.description: System.out.println("auth: issued token " + session.token + " for " + owner) ships the live bearer token to the service's standard log on every issue(). Anything that ingests stdout (log shippers, journald, debug consoles, error reporters) gets a full session token; log retention and access become the de-facto auth boundary.

findings.title: Failed-auth response echoes the presented token
findings.description: When verify() returns null the handler writes 'unauthorized: unknown token (token ' + token + ')' into the 401 body. Tokens are echoed back to the caller, which both confirms a token is well-formed and helps an attacker correlate probed tokens against the response — turning blind brute force into a cheap search.

findings.title: byOwner uses substring match, leaking adjacent owners
findings.description: byOwner(owner) returns every link where link.owner.contains(owner). Querying 'a' returns links owned by 'alice', 'alicia', 'anna', and 'a' itself, so any authenticated caller can enumerate other tenants' link codes by feeding single characters or short prefixes. That is an information-disclosure primitive across the multi-tenant boundary.

findings.title: writeSnapshot writes to a hard-coded /tmp path
findings.description: writeSnapshot() always stages the snapshot at /tmp/linkd-snapshot.json before renaming it into dir. On a multi-tenant box a local attacker can pre-create /tmp/linkd-snapshot.json as a symlink to an arbitrary file and have the rename() land there, or race the temp file's contents between the write and the rename.

findings.title: bearerToken crashes on missing/malformed header
findings.description: bearerToken() does header.split(" ") and returns parts[1] with no length or prefix check. A request with no Authorization header NPEs on the null receiver; a header without a space AIOOBEs on parts[1]. Main.authenticate() calls it on every protected endpoint, so missing headers turn into 500s instead of 401s — a low-effort unauthenticated DoS against any write/read endpoint.

findings.title: requireAdmin() always rejects (and is never called)
findings.description: The condition !role.equals("admin") || !role.equals("owner") is true for every String — a value cannot equal two distinct strings at once — so the method returns false for every session. It is dead code today, but the broken logic is the smoking gun for why the /admin/quotas endpoint fell back to a header check instead of using session.role. The next caller who wires it in will ship a permanent lockout, and the only reason admin auth looks 'sort of working' is the X-Admin header bypass.
